r: Only Congress can create provinces and cities because doing so creates legislative districts; the power to reapportion is part of national legislative power and cannot be delegated to a regional assembly. ARMM’s law creating Shariff Kabunsuan was void. The Constitution is silent on any such power for autonomous regions (expressio unius est exclusio alterius), and a regional assembly legislates only on regional matters within its territory. The ARMM may still create municipalities and barangays, which do not create legislative districts.
f: The ARMM Regional Assembly created the province of Shariff Kabunsuan under a delegation in the ARMM Organic Act. COMELEC Resolution 7902 then kept Shariff Kabunsuan and Cotabato City together as Maguindanao’s first district; Sema, a congressional candidate there, argued the new province was entitled to its own representative.
h: The delegation and the creation of the province were void. COMELEC Resolution 7902 was valid because it merely kept the existing district.
x: Use when a body other than Congress tries to create districts or change Congress’s composition.
g: Gatmaytan’s book: an inferior legislative body created by a superior one cannot change the superior’s membership.
s: Only Congress may create legislative districts, so only Congress creates provinces and cities.

r: The power to create local government units is legislative. Absence of a Local Government Code with criteria did not stop the legislature from creating a municipality, subject to a plebiscite. Once the Code is enacted, creations must meet its criteria; in the interregnum the legislature’s power is plenary, subject only to approval by the people concerned in a plebiscite. Sibagat’s creation was approved in a plebiscite and its officers had assumed office, so it was a de jure municipality.
f: BP 56 created the Municipality of Sibagat before the Local Government Code was enacted. Petitioners invoked Art. XI, Sec. 3 of the 1973 Constitution, which required a Local Government Code to set the criteria for creating local units; no such Code existed when BP 56 was passed.
x: Plenary legislative power except as limited by the Constitution.

n: ABAKADA Guro Party List v. Purisima
r: Once a law is enacted, Congress’s role is limited to scrutiny and investigation. A Joint Congressional Oversight Committee empowered to approve the IRR is a legislative veto: it lets Congress take part in implementing the law, violates separation of powers, and bypasses bicameralism and presentment. The rest of RA 9335 was upheld through the separability clause.
f: RA 9335 (Attrition Act) gave BIR and BOC personnel rewards for exceeding revenue targets and created a JCOC to approve its IRR.
h: The JCOC approval provision (Sec. 12) was void; the reward system and the rest of the law stood.
x: The 2023 midterm (Tax Code Sec. 290-A oversight committee on illicit trade): ask whether the committee merely reviews and recommends (valid scrutiny) or approves, deputizes, or directs implementation (invalid). Also any bicam or law clause requiring congressional approval of IRRs.
test: Valid oversight: (1) scrutiny (budget hearings, question hour, confirmation); (2) investigation in aid of legislation. Invalid: supervision or any post-enactment approval, veto, or role in execution.
g: Gatmaytan’s book treats legislative vetoes as the textbook violation of separation of powers (‘an inward-turning delegation’ attaching a congressional leash). He also criticizes tying severability to separability clauses, citing ABAKADA.
s: After enactment Congress may only scrutinize and investigate; a JCOC approving IRRs is a legislative veto.

r: A title must not mislead. ‘An Act creating the Municipality of Dianaton in Lanao del Sur’ hid that the law also took barrios from Cotabato. The whole law was void because the valid and invalid parts could not be separated. A title is defective if it misleads, is too restrictive, or fails to reflect essential matters in the law; it must lead legislators and the public to inquire into the body and so prevent surprise or fraud. Dianaton was premised on all 21 barrios, so removing the 12 Cotabato barrios would change its viability and the legislative intent.
f: RA 4790’s body included twelve barrios of Cotabato province in a new Lanao del Sur town.
h: RA 4790 declared void in its entirety.
x: Title and one-subject rule: dual purposes (no hodgepodge; the title must inform legislators and the public).
test: Title rule complied with if the title is comprehensive enough to include the general object, and all parts are germane to it; it is violated if the title misleads or the body includes a subject not fairly embraced.
s: A misleading title voids the law; inseparable parts fall together.

r: A municipality given power to ‘regulate’ businesses cannot prohibit a lawful business outright; the amending law’s title spoke only of regulation, and a construction that keeps the law constitutional is preferred. The Bocaue ordinance closing all night clubs was unreasonable.
f: Bocaue, Bulacan passed a ‘Prohibition and Closure Ordinance’ banning night clubs and cabarets. The enabling law (RA 938) was titled as a grant of power to ‘regulate’; a later amendment let municipalities ‘prohibit or regulate’ in the body, but the title was not changed.
x: Titles limit what a law can be read to authorize; police power by LGUs must be reasonable (regulate, not prohibit).

r: The Fair Election Act’s repeal of the rule that elective officials are deemed resigned upon filing a COC is germane to its title on fair and honest elections; titles are construed liberally so as not to cripple legislation. The title need not be a complete index of the contents; any number of provisions are valid if they are not foreign to the general subject and serve as means of carrying it out. The record showed Congress deliberately framed the title to cover election reforms beyond lifting the political ad ban.
f: Petitioners argued that Sections 12 and 14 of RA 9006 were riders unrelated to lifting the political ad ban.
x: Rider and title challenges: liberal construction; germaneness.
